newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan recognises Taleban Afghan government.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan recognises Taleban Afghan government.

text.p: Pakistan appeared to signal its recognition on Friday of the new Taleban militia government in neighbouring Afghanistan after the militia's earlier capture of Kabul, and called for restraint and peace talks there.

"In keeping with its policy, the government of Pakistan will send immediately a delegation to establish contact with the new government in Kabul and maintain its contact with the Taleban Shura (council) in (the southern town of) Kandahar," a foreign ministry statement said.

Diplomatic sources said the statement's wording about dealing with a "new government" amounted to a recognition of the Taleban administration by Pakistan, which would make it the first country to do so.
A Taleban spokesman in Kandahar earlier said the militia government should be recognised by the world because it controlled the Afghan capital and most of the country.

The Taleban entered Kabul around 1.00 a.m. (2130 GMT Thursday), hours after it had been abandoned by govenrment troops, and appeared to be in full control, hanging a former president and his brother and proclaiming an Islamic state.

The Pakistan Foreign Ministry statement said that "a qualitatively new situation" had been created by the takeover in Kabul by the Taleban, which swept away President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government there.

Pakistan's priority would be "to impress upon the new government the need for restraint and for maintenance of conditions for the unimpeded flow of humanitarian assistance to the population of Kabul," the statement said.
"It will also urge the need for such dialogue as may promote peace in all areas of Afghanistan," the statement said.

Pakistan has not reopened its embassy in Kabul after the mission building was sacked and burned by a mob protesting Islamabad's alleged support for Taleban when the militia captured the main western town of Herat.

Pakistan's top Foreign Ministry official, secretary Najmuddin Sheikh was to have visited Kabul on September 19 to reopen the embassy, but he postponed the trip after Kabul resumed its charges of interference against Islamabad.
Pakistan has repeatedly denied the charges and said it has no favourites among the Afghan factions, most of which it helped in their guerrilla war against Soviet occupation in the 1980s.
The Foreign Ministry statement said Islamabad had urged the Taleban to spare the life of ex-president Najibullah, who was hanged in Kabul on Friday morning, but it was too late.
Najibullah and his brother Shahpur Ahmadzai were executed in the early hours of the morning after being dragged out of a U.N. compound in Kabul, where they had taken shelter for more than four years.
The Pakistani statement said Islamabad was informed through New York at 7.00 a.m. (0200 gmt) that Najibullah had been taken out of the compound.

"An appeal for his safety by the United Nations was immediately conveyed to the Taleban Shura in Kandahar by the government of Pakistan through its consulate general, which added its own strong endorsement for protecting Najibullah. At that time we were informed that the Shura was only aware of Najibullah's arrest," the statement said.
